The terms ''a priori'' ("from the earlier") and ''a posteriori'' ("from the later") are used in [[philosophy]] ([[epistemology]]) to distinguish two types of [[knowledge]],  justification, or [[argument]]:
* ''A priori'' knowledge or justification is independent of [[experience]] (for example "All bachelors are unmarried"). Galen Strawson has stated that an ''a priori'' argument is one in which "you can see that it is [[Truth|true]] just lying on your couch.  You don't have to get up off your couch and go outside and examine the way things are in the physical world.  You don't have to do any science.";<ref name="Galen Strawson interviewed by Tamler Sommers">Sommers, Tamler (2003)</ref>
* ''A posteriori'' knowledge or justification is dependent on [[experience]] or [[empirical evidence]] (for example "Some bachelors are very unhappy").

An ''a priori language'' is any [[constructed language]] whose [[vocabulary]] is not based on existing languages, unlike ''[[a posteriori (languages)|a posteriori]]'' constructed languages.  Examples of ''a priori'' languages include [[Lojban]], [[Loglan]], [[Ro (language)|Ro]], [[Solresol]], [[Mirad]],  [[Klingon language|Klingon]], [[Ithkuil]], [[Na'vi language|Na'vi]], and [[Valyrian languages|High Valyrian]]. By contrast, ''a posteriori'' languages are ones whose vocabulary is based on existing languages, either as a variation of one language (e.g., [[Latino sine flexione]]) or as a mixture of various languages (e.g., [[Esperanto]]).
